newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia tells banks how to fight money-laundering.
newsitem.headline: Russia tells banks how to fight money-laundering.

text.p: Russia's central bank said on Wednesday it had given commercial banks new rules to help fight money laundering but feared the measures would only slow down a growing trend rather than reverse it.

Money laundering has become an open secret since Russia began its lurch into market reforms at the start of the decade. It was less apparent under Soviet rule, when commercial banks did not exist and access to international markets was limited.

"It is only natural that (the amount of money-laundering) is increasing," Deputy Chairman Alexander Turbanov told a news conference. "The dynamics will go further up. It is a real and natural process.
"But we can forecast that by introducing the measures against money laundering and strengthening the banking system we are creating guarantees that banks will not become a criminalised world."
Russia does not yet have a law on money laundering.
Turbanov said the central bank, which issued its guidelines on July 3, did not have figures for the volume of money-laundering. But he said police estimates were too high.

Vladimir Smirnov, head of the currency operations control department at the central bank, said British banks every year reported 18,000 deals they found suspicious to the police and they investigated 3,000 cases.
He said he expected the number of cases in Russia to be not less than that.
Turbanov said the central bank would monitor how well banks followed the measures but could not punish those which did not.
It will collect information on banks and take a closer look at them if they fail to comply with other demands.
The rules applied to foreign banks registered in Russia, too, he said.
The rules require banks to look more closely at their clients and report to the police any transaction which has a monthly volume exceeding or equalling 1,000 times the minimum wages for individuals.
In the case of company transactions, the trigger point would be if the volume was greater than 10,000 times the minimum wage.
Russia's minimum monthly wage is 83,490 roubles ($14.45).

Turbanov said so far there was no police protection for banking employees who reported suspicious cases. But he said the bank was aiming to find ways to solve this problem. The government would not be liable for damages if an investigation was subsequently dropped. ($=5,776 roubles)
